This opening includes the usual parts of a letter: 

- sender, 

- recipient, and 

- greeting. 

Additional details emphasize Paul's important message (see also {{Romans 1:1-7|Romans 1:1–7}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:1-3|1 Corinthians 1:1–3}}; {{Galatians 1:1-5|Galatians 1:1–5}}; {{Titus 1:1-4|Titus 1:1–4}}).
B

Paul had authority because God had commanded him to be an apostle. Using this authority, Paul commanded Timothy to stay in Ephesus and keep working there.

Part of Timothy’s work was to command people to stop teaching things that weren’t true. The purpose of the commands was love. Paul gave Timothy his command because he loved Timothy and the church in Ephesus. Timothy would show his love for the church in Ephesus by correcting the false teachings.

When people believe true teaching about Jesus, God’s love grows strong among them. Some believers in Ephesus taught religious stories and ideas that weren’t about Jesus. They also taught about Jewish laws without understanding them.

Paul explained that the Law of Moses showed people what not to do. But the law couldn’t make people do what they should do. God makes people able to do what they should do. The Holy Spirit works in the hearts of those who have faith in God. He helps them to know what is honest, right and true.

- Timothy was in Ephesus as Paul's representative (see 1 Timothy Book Introduction, “Setting”).

- *my true child: *Timothy was like a true child to Paul in the faith (see {{Philippians 2:20|Philippians 2:20}}; compare {{Titus 1:4|Titus 1:4}}). But he was probably not directly converted by Paul (see {{Acts 16:1|Acts 16:1}}).
T
*not to teach false doctrines*: As Paul had warned before, false teachers entered the church in Ephesus ({{Acts 20:29-31|Acts 20:29–31}}). He wrote this letter to help Timothy deal with them.

Paul's greetings usually include a mention of thanks or blessing to God. Greco-Roman letters were often structured this way. First Timothy and Titus probably do not include this because they are official letters authorizing a delegate (see 1 Timothy Book Introduction, “Literary Genre”). Instead, Paul first addresses his concern about stopping false teachers.

- *myths and endless genealogies … speculation*: Paul might be dismissing their teachings as not significant, or he might rejecting their interpretations and their justification of bad behavior ({{1 Timothy 1:7|1:7}}; see also {{2 Timothy 4:3-4|2 Timothy 4:3–4}}; {{Titus 1:14|Titus 1:14}}; {{Titus 3:9|3:9}}; {{2 Peter 1:16|2 Peter 1:16}}; {{1 Timothy 1:8-11|1 Timothy 1:8–11}}; {{1 Timothy 4:1-2|4:1–2}}, {{1 Timothy 4:7|7}}; see also {{Titus 1:15-16|Titus 1:15–16}}).

- *endless genealogies*: In Judaism, a genealogy (list of ancestors) established a person's spiritual heritage. The false teachers might have focused too much on this. As the church leader, Timothy was to treat other believers like family members. They were fathers, mothers, sisters and brothers in God’s family. They all had needs and should help take care of one another.

Paul took special care to talk about widows in the church. Church elders were one kind of leader. They were to be respected for serving the church faithfully. When they sinned, it had to be dealt with fairly. This was because the church must be a faithful witness to everyone about Jesus.

Even when leaders serve Jesus faithfully, people might accuse them of doing wrong. Paul explained a fair system. This system would protect church elders if they were falsely accused. Paul also warned Timothy to be careful about appointing new leaders. Appointing leaders was done by placing hands on people. This set them apart to be leaders who served.

Church leaders must be completely committed to turning away from sin. Paul reminded Timothy that no sins stay hidden for ever. Sooner or later people face judgement for their sins. Good works that people do will also be seen and recognised by others.

This was true even in how slaves and slave owners treated one another. Slaves who followed Jesus were to serve their masters with respect. Slave owners were to take good care of those who served them.

Some believers in Ephesus liked to cause trouble by disagreeing and arguing. Others thought that following Jesus was a way to get rich. Loving money and trying to get more of it led them to do evil things.

Paul told Timothy not to be like those people. Instead, he should be firm in teaching the truth about Jesus as Lord and King. Paul made it very clear that following Jesus doesn’t lead people to grow rich. Faithful believers learn to be thankful for what they have and to be happy with it.

Timothy was to warn rich believers not to trust in their money. Instead they were to share freely and put their hope in God. Paul explained that following Jesus brings something much better than riches on earth. When Jesus returns his faithful followers will live with him for ever. That is what Paul called the life that really is life.

Paul emphasizes the historical aspect of Christ's role as a mediator (see {{1 Timothy 2:5-6|2:5–6}}). Paul holds up the way Christ Jesus testified during his trial before Pontius Pilate to set an example for Timothy to remain strong under pressure ({{Matthew 27:11-14|Matthew 27:11–14}}; {{Luke 23:1-4|Luke 23:1–4}}; {{John 18:33-38|John 18:33–38}}; {{John 19:9-11|19:9–11}}).

*until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ*: The letters to Timothy and Titus describe Christ's comings, both past and future, as “epiphanies” or “appearances” ({{2 Timothy 1:10|2 Timothy 1:10}}; {{Titus 2:11|Titus 2:11}}; {{2 Timothy 4:1|2 Timothy 4:1}}, {{2 Timothy 4:8|8}}; {{Titus 2:13|Titus 2:13}}). An epiphany is a divine intervention at a specific historical moment. The church exists between these past and future appearances of Christ. 

Christ’s first saving epiphany allowed for a new life. His future epiphany will bring final salvation. Although the present is evil, our anticipation of Christ’s appearance encourages us to live a life pleasing to God now (the “later times,” {{1 Timothy 4:1-3|1 Timothy 4:1–3}}; {{2 Timothy 3:1-9|2 Timothy 3:1–9}}). False teachers allowed sinful behaviors because they believed the resurrection had already happened ({{2 Timothy 2:18|2 Timothy 2:18}}). Paul clarifies that salvation has started but is not yet complete. Being part of God’s household requires responsible conduct in the light of Christ’s past, present, and future saving work ({{1 Timothy 3:15-16|1 Timothy 3:15–16}}; {{Titus 2:11-14|Titus 2:11–14}}).

- *in his own time:* At the right time, God will complete the salvation promised to us before the world began (compare {{1 Timothy 2:6|2:6}}); {{2 Timothy 1:9|2 Timothy 1:9}}; {{Titus 1:2|Titus 1:2}}). Christ began this salvation in his first appearance ({{1 Timothy 2:6|1 Timothy 2:6}}; {{Titus 1:3|Titus 1:3}}). Christ's work of salvation fits within God's eternal plans. This knowledge naturally leads to worshiping God who saves us (see {{1 Timothy 1:17|1 Timothy 1:17}}).

It includes an entire way of life ({{2 Timothy 1:13-14|2 Timothy 1:13–14}}; {{2 Timothy 3:10-11|3:10–11}}). It strengthens and cleanses the church when confronted with false teachings in challenging times ({{2 Timothy 3:1|2 Timothy 3:1}}).
